articles.title: Writing a Demoscene Intro for the ZX Spectrum
articles.content: In the late 80s, I spent an embarrassing number of hours hunched over my ZX Spectrum, typing in Sinclair BASIC programs and rudimentary assembler routines copied from magazines, trying to re-create the Amiga crack intros I’d seen round at a friend’s house. Obviously, they never came even slightly close - but now, many decades later, I’ve finally managed it! I’m now the proud author of a hand-rolled retro demoscene intro that runs on a stock 128Kb Spectrum. It features all those late 80s tropes: A smooth scrolltext (with ‘leet custom fonts!), a three-channel AY soundtrack, bouncing VU meters and the essential parallax starfield. It’s currently 10287 bytes of code, or 19552 bytes as a complete tape image - which, given I’ve been working on this since December 13th last year, means my average rate of code-production is a paltry ~ 455 bytes per week! This blog post is a technical overview of how I got there, some cool tricks I picked up, and everything I had to learn (and re-learn) about the Speccy and Z80 assembly along the way. It simultaneously rates as one of my favourite side-projects ever, and also the one that most often nearly triggered a foot put through my monitor in frustration. I’ll reflect on all that at the end , but for now if you just want to see the finished product, the download button is at the top of the article and the included .tap cassette tape image should load into any emulator. There’s also a YouTube capture , links to the production on pouet.net , and you can run it from within a web browser by visiting my TNFS site portal - check option 4 for recent uploads. Be Kind, Rewind But let’s skip back briefly to the late 80s. Coming from the world of an 8-bit, cassette tape loading computer, seeing an Amiga for the first time was like encountering something from outer space. Like everyone who saw one back in the day, I was blown away by the amazing graphics and sound on display, not to mention the library of ground-breaking games . But I found myself even more captivated by the mysterious (and totally badass) “intros” displayed at the beginning of pirated games. Created by the software piracy groups that had cracked the copy protection and distributed the floppy-disk based games, they were mini works of art in their own right - music, graphics and usually some cool-looking effect to show off the group’s prowess. There’s a great collection of these intros (or “cracktros”) archived on YouTube . Watch a few of those videos and you’ll quickly notice the “design” tropes that almost every cracktro shares: a cool, edgy logo at the top of the screen (bonus points if it’s dripping blood or in any way “metal”), some boastful text displayed on top of an effect of some sort - usually a scrolling parallax starfield, or rotating 3d object - and a further scroll-text full of shout outs, greetings to fellow pseudonymous crackers and adverts for illegal BBS systems galore. articles.title: A Modern Web App in C
articles.content: ## INTRO If you wanted a dynamic website in 1994, you wrote a C program, dropped it in a cgi-bin directory, and let Apache fork it per request. Thirty-two years later, I shipped a commercial web product using fundamentally the same technology. Everything about marketyour.games is modern. It's a web product with user accounts, a search dashboard for content creators, folders for organizing them, payments via Stripe and transactional emails via Postmark. It follows progressive enhancement and doesn't require any JavaScript. Everything is modern except the way it was made and how it is served. Here are my thoughts on writing a real product in C and serving it via CGI in 2026. ## TLDR CGI's decline was justified in 2004 but doesn't hold up in 2026. You can write a modern web application in C. I shipped one. One binary, a SQLite file, three dependencies and the entire thing fits in your head. ## HOW IT WAS DONE The stack is BCHS : OpenBSD, C, httpd, and SQLite. There's no framework. You write a C program that reads CGI environment variables and responds. There's no templating language. You write C that outputs the HTML directly. There's no separate database server. You open the database file through SQLite's C API. There's no container. You build a statically linked binary and drop it in a folder. Every request spawns a fresh process. Deploying a new version is replacing one file. That means no server restart and no downtime. New requests simply pick up the new binary. OpenBSD ships with sane defaults and gives you the tools to actually secure a C program like pledge and unveil. Httpd serves from a chroot by default, so your CGI binary runs sandboxed to its own corner of the filesystem. I lean on three additional libraries: libcurl handles all outbound requests to Stripe and Postmark. libsodium handles random identifier generation, password hashing and the HMAC verification for Stripe webhooks. libcjson handles JSON parsing for Stripe and Postmark. Only two of those are actual build dependencies: libcurl and libsodium. libcjson is a single C file and has no external dependencies. SQLite ships an official amalgamation (single C file) build. Both are vendored and built as part of the project. The result is a build with almost no moving parts. A clean build takes a few seconds and rebuilds complete in less than half a second. Instead of serving static assets the traditional way, I route all traffic from httpd to the CGI binary. Every asset is compiled into the executable and served from memory. ## WHAT I LIKED Fundamentals over frameworks. CGI isn't a framework to learn. The 1.1 specification was published in 2004 and hasn't changed since. There's no API to internalize. The entire interface is a handful of fundamental HTTP concepts: Request headers. Request methods. Query strings. Body data. If you understand HTTP, you already understand CGI. It's language and platform agnostic. You learn it once and the knowledge is good forever. Clear separation of con

articles.title: Who is vfmaddrnd231pd?
articles.content: Who is vfmaddrnd231pd?? October 12, 2026 vfmaddrnd231pd is a unique instruction from the FMA instruction set. Most instructions in that set have mnemonics like vfmadd231pd , but here rnd means something very specific. The Intel Software Development Manual documents it as: VFMADDRND231PD – Fused Multiply-Add of Packed Double-Precision Floating-Point Values with rounding control […] The immediate byte defines several bit fields that control rounding, DAZ, FTZ, and exception suppression (See Table 5-3). Most x86 floating-point instructions use the global rounding mode and settings, changing which is pretty slow. But vfmaddrnd231pd allows the rounding mode to be controlled on a per-instruction basis, and since FMA can emulate addition, subtraction, and multiplication, this mechanism effectively allows any arithmetic to have controllable rounding without AVX-512 – making some algorithms that rely on rounding incredibly faster. Or so it would , if this instruction actually existed. GNU assembler doesn’t recognize it. The Intel C/C++ Compiler intrinsics _mm_fmaddround_pd and _mm256_fmaddround_pd that SDM mentions are absent not only from Clang, but from ICC as well. Trying to assemble the instructions by hand from the SDM opcode list reveals another issue: VEX.DDS.128.66.0F3A.W1 B8 /r /ib VEX is the VEX prefix, but what is DDS ? This opcode is the only mention of DDS in the SDM, and this SO answer says that DDS is merely used for documentation and was removed from later SDM versions, but the fact that it’s still present here is suspicious. And when you actually run the instruction on a CPU that supports the FMA instruction set, like my Haswell, it raises #UD (“UnDefined instruction”)! I already found it strange that the SDM only lists vfmaddrnd231pd and not other variants like using pd / ps / sd / ss or 132 / 213 / 231 , which other FMA instructions have, but this confirmed my suspicions. It was at that point that I downloaded a more recent version of the SDM and noticed that this instruction is absent in the 2026 edition of the SDM, despite being present in the 2024 version. I must say I’m incredibly confused. This instruction doesn’t look like a typo in the documentation, since the docs contain unique tables and pseudocode that isn’t similar to any other instruction. My best hypothesis is that Intel wanted to add the vfmaddrnd* set, then found an issue with it at the last moment and removed it from the CPU, but didn’t quite adjust the SDM correctly. But I have no way to confirm that. If anyone reading this has a friend at Intel, I’d love to know the answer.

articles.title: Hackers activate automatic defrosting in supermarket fridges across Europe
articles.content: An ongoing cyberattack has reportedly struck major supermarket chains across Europe, disrupting refrigeration control systems. The attack — which has reportedly seen units set to continuously defrost at 50 degrees Celsius — is also apparently affecting deliveries and in-store pricing powered by electronic shelf labels, La Dépêche reports . According to the report, "several" major retailers have been targeted by a cyberattack, which has hit Danfoss-made refrigeration controls used by French supermarkets Intermarché, Leclerc, and Coopérative U. Indeed, the latter's president, Dominique Schelcher, has confirmed as of Monday morning that "A cyberattack has been affecting the refrigeration production facilities of several stores in our network since last night." Schelcher said teams had been mobilized to fix the issue and promised an investigation into the incident, which he described as "extremely serious." The report states the units have had their automatic defrosting systems activate, but that hackers have also configured the function — which normally runs for just two hours a day — into a continuous, forced defrosting cycle with the temperature set to a toasty 50 degrees Celsius. Sources reportedly described "a wave of heat" escaping from fridges and freezers Early reports indicate losses are already approaching 300,000 euros, but could run into several million euros nationwide. Separately, NOS in the Netherlands reports that several supermarket chains have been hit with a malfunction due to a cybersecurity incident on Sunday afternoon. Albert Heijn, Etos, and Gall & Gall have had their websites taken down, impacting deliveries. Electronic shelf labels have also been compromised, disrupting in-store pricing. "We have immediately taken measures to protect our IT environment. Part of this involves the preventive temporary shutdown of a number of systems," Albert Heijn said in a statement. It is unclear at this stage whether the two attacks are related or how widespread either of them is. Belgium's Delhaize chain, which belongs to Albert Heijn, has also reported disruption. Images online show stores in Amsterdam warning customers about price problems, and the suspension of loyalty programs that have also been impacted by the incident. articles.title: Making big downloads resumable in Firefox
articles.content: Navigation Making big downloads resumable in firefox For whatever reason, Firefox 28 and newer (i.e. every modern version after like 2014 ) ships with network.http.response.timeout set to 300 seconds. This seems to interfere with resuming big downloads, as well as the general stability of big downloads. Setting network.http.response.timeout to 0 (or something very big) in about:config seems to make big downloads both resumable and at least a little more stable. I don't understand why this works, but experimental testing supports it. Note that this assumes the server supports resumable downloads; if it doesn't, no settings in firefox or any other browser are going to help. However, the problem this fixes is firefox being unable to resume a resumable download on error. I don't entirely know if this is the case, but it experimentally looks like resumable downloads in firefox rely on connection timeouts rather than the .part files they download. Firefox will happily ignore an existing .part without this option, and I do not understand why. Resumable downloads in firefox generally appear to be fairly unstable though. This has been a known problem in some form since as far back as 2005 . I also found that there's a manual .part shuffle to make firefox actually resume downloads , but I'm not doing that shit. As a non-firefox workaround, using wget -c -O "$filename" "$url" also works, and wget overall appears to be fairly stable. I do also suspect firefox does some hidden retries if it can before it considers the download to have failed - from some experimental testing, it does appear that this is at least partly related to network.http.response.timeout , and that exceeding the timeout interferes with this process. I have not attempted to confirm any of this with FF's source code, because I have no clue where to look.

articles.title: Turn a WiFi 7 Router into a 320Msps Software Defined Radio Receiver
articles.content: Turns a Gemtek W1700K Wi-Fi 7 router into a wideband software-defined receiver. The router's MediaTek MT7996 radio captures raw 14-bit IQ at up to 320 Msps, its Airoha AN7581 SoC streams it over 10 GbE, and a Linux host shows it as a live spectrum and waterfall in the browser, with the receiver's controls next to it. The whole 2.4 GHz band at 320 Msps, live, with the decimation's roll-off corrected in the stream ("flatten"): a 262,144-point FFT of every sample, 100 spectra a second (this recording runs at 50 frames a second). The MT7996 runs only our own firmware: a ROM patch, WM and WA built from this repository, with no MediaTek code. It brings the radio up from a cold power-on by itself, from MediaTek's initialisation and calibration decoded register by register against a trace of MediaTek's own firmware, and takes its commands (LO, sample rate, capture, stream, gain, filter) from the host. articles.title: Living in the Weimar era of Ruby
articles.content: Much has been said about the DHH keynote that he gave at RailsWorld. To me, it was the voice of a person in an existential crisis, but also a very jaded one. “Look how I don’t care anymore, and you should not care either” is not a great message when you are the headline speaker at the conference - let’s call it CareConf - that you have, yourself, lobbied for. The message from the supreme leader was clear: we vibe-rewrote HEY in a more performant way, it worked great, we neither need nor care about Rails anymore. I honestly believe that, instead of amassing even more applause via vitriolic truth-bombing, he could have just left the toy he no longer loves - including its community - in peace. But here is the thing: the rich and famous losing interest in the good stuff does not oblige the rest of us to. If anything, it frees up the room. 🧭 I am currently available for contract work. Hire me to help make your Rails app better! I must admit that for a few days I felt very depressed about it all. Not about “AIs writing all the code” - that much is clear to me, and I do not lament the changing landscape of the craft - I do lament the landscape of usage , which is a topic for another article. It is abundantly clear that the LLMs are here to stay, that typing every single line by hand is no longer sustainable, and that the scales have shifted profoundly. What made me depressed was just how little care there was about the Ruby ecosystem and community, and the disdain with which David flushed the entire Rails and Ruby culture down the drain for the sake of “running it on a single Raspberry Pi”, as he put it. What I am actually observing is something different: a renaissance, even though quite a few prominent Rubyists have moved on to other stacks - which are now much more open to exploration, as you don’t have to write all that… gunk - let’s call it what it is - by hand. A detailed unpack of 7 little-endian integers is not particularly interesting, nor artistic - it’s just gunk, and I won’t miss it. Unless struct packing is needed to make it fast, but then we can always art-direct additionally. There was an interesting time in German history, right between the two World Wars - the “interbellum”, the time of the Weimar Republic. It was very turbulent, and a lot of it wasn’t pretty in the slightest - social difficulties, unemployment, incredible inflation, squalid living conditions, the emergence of the wildest movements, cabarets and cults imaginable… but there was also something else. The “Roaring Twenties” of Weimar Germany also produced an incredible number of great, whimsical, fascinating artistic movements. From the Bauhaus to the Berlin gay cabarets, from Kurt Weill to Fritz Lang’s Metropolis - it was a booming time, and a lot of what appeared then is still valued and cherished today. And it was a technological boom as well - the ever more widespread use of electricity, the large-scale deployment of modern pharmaceuticals, the subways, the automobile…

articles.title: Linus Torvalds Working On A Hefty Linux Kernel Improvement With Claude Code
articles.content: Linux creator Linus Torvalds has been known to use AI to help with kernel debugging and outside of the kernel tree has also done some vibe coding with Google's Antigravity . He has previously said he views AI as a useful tool . It turns out he's even now using Claude Code for working on new Linux kernel features. While waiting for the Linux 7.3-rc7 kernel release and refreshing his torvalds/linux.git repository, I was surprised to find a new kernel branch appear. Typically Torvalds isn't doing much work on branches in his main repository and typically just hosting the master branch. The new branch to appear is noref-filemap-read-with-llm and as implied by the "LLM" postfix, is some new kernel improvements he's been working on with the help of AI / LLMs. Claude Code in particular. The branched code is working on adapting the memory management code to read from the page cache without folio references. The code is working on addressing a Linux issue of small reads of one file from many threads contend on the folio reference counting. So the goal of the branch / patch series is to read from the page cache without folio references. For those passionate about AI for loving or hating it, in the main patch message Linus Torvalds confirmed his AI use in creating this work and related testing and even the initial draft of the cover letter: "The code, the test programs, the review behind the list above and the first draft of this text were done with an LLM coding assistant (Claude Code) under my direction. The measurements were run on my machine." And for the impact on this situation of addressing the bottleneck of small reads of one file from many threads, the impact of the series is significant: Quite a difference. The patches are currently on Torvalds' noref-filemap-read-with-llm Git branch . We'll see if he merges his branch for the upcoming Linux 7.4 merge window. articles.title: (Post-Quantum) Cryptographic Right Answers
articles.content: Publishing “Cryptographic Right Answers” for developers is a tradition by now. Colin Percival started in 2009 , Thomas Ptacek followed up in 2015 , and then Latacora carried on in 2018 and 2024 . It might feel too soon for an update, but so much has changed . The timeline of the post-quantum transition dramatically shifted in early 2026 , and there is now consensus that it needs to complete by 2029. 2029! We have three years! The good news is that, despite what you might have heard, symmetric cryptography is going to be fine, because Grover does not matter . The bad news is that all asymmetric answers changed compared to 2018 and most even compared to 2024. The answers below assume you are not constrained by any specific compliance regime, although they are mostly compatible with FIPS 140. If you need to follow something stricter like CNSA 2.0, you’ll know. Just substitute as appropriate. Finally, remember the other big change of 2026: LLMs are very good at finding bugs now. “Get a review from the best model you can afford” is now firmly a Cryptographic Right Answer, along with the long-time classic “use a memory-safe language.” If you’re in a rush, here’s the cheat sheet: Encrypting data : If you’re in the cloud, KMS. Otherwise, XAES-256-GCM or XChaCha20Poly1305 with random nonces. If you’re encrypting more than a few MB, use Cobblestone-128. Symmetric key length : Don’t stress it. 256-bit keys if you need to pick. Symmetric “signatures” : HMAC-SHA-256. Hash algorithm : SHA-2 is still fine, but use a real multihash (SequenceHash) if needed. Random IDs : 32 random bytes, a.k.a. 256-bit random numbers. Password handling : Argon2id or scrypt. But have you considered passkeys instead? Key exchange : X25519+ML-KEM-768 in a secure, standard protocol. Asymmetric encryption : HPKE with (MLKEM768-X25519 a.k.a. X-Wing, HKDF-SHA256, AES-128-GCM), or age with PQ keys. Asymmetric signatures : ML-DSA-44. Website or client-server application security : If you’re in the cloud, use its ALB/NLB. Otherwise, rustls, Go’s crypto/tls, BoringSSL, AWS-LC, or s2n-tls with a popular, updated ACME client. Online backups : restic with a long random password. Now let’s dive in. Encrypting data If you’re in the cloud, KMS . Otherwise, XAES-256-GCM or XChaCha20Poly1305 with random nonces. If you’re encrypting more than a few MB, use Cobblestone-128 . Percival, 2009 : AES-CTR with HMAC. Ptacek, 2015 : NaCl/libsodium default, or ChaCha20Poly1305, or AES-GCM. Latacora, 2018 : KMS, or XSalsa20+Poly1305. Latacora, 2024 : KMS, or NaCl’s secretbox, or XChaCha20Poly1305. Latacora’s reasoning for why and when you’d use your cloud’s KMS is still solid, so start there. If you’re encrypting locally, you want an AEAD where you can avoid worrying about tracking nonces or how many messages you encrypted, so you want random nonces of at least 128 bits. NaCl/libsodium’s secretbox is just a paper-thin wrapper around a less common AE construction (XSalsa20+Poly1305), so instead I recommend XAES

articles.title: 'AI' is Not a Tool
articles.content: (I keep delivering this as a quip, here's a bit more) First order of business - is ' tool ' going to have an interesting, distinguishing and thus illuminative meaning or be a mere platitudinous stand-in for "anything useful"? We'll save tool as "anyone/thing that can be exploited" for the AI titans, for whom VCs, politicians, wannabe-titan-CEOs, software devs, rural towns etc are all 'tools'. The pockets on the front of my shirts are useful (I need to keep my reading glasses handy), but they are not tools. Similarly, fast food drive-thru windows are useful, but are not tools (more later). Some definitions of ' tool ': a device or implement, especially one held in the hand, used to carry out a particular function an instrument (such as a hammer or saw) used or worked by hand : an instrument used by a handicraftsperson or laborer in their work What I like best - A tool is something you wield . wield - to use (as a tool or instrument) especially with full command or power : handle, manipulate, control Especially useful in that are: Held in your hand - a source of both control and feedback, and an indication of the intimacy of the act of use Power - force, energy transmission and direction, leverage etc Control - intention and continuous directing of the course of events Tools are implements with which you do something, they do not do things for you. Tool use builds, rewards, and often requires, expertise and skill. The continuous application of technique and energy, and sensory feedback, are essential to the buildup of expertise (from experiri - "try"). Good tools have many properties LLMs lack - they are predictable, reliable, deterministic, of bounded function, hopefully simple etc. What you learn while wielding a tool is something about the world, the task, the physics, logic etc of what you are trying to do or the situation you are trying to overcome. And often, something about yourself. As a lifelong tool builder and user, I know what tools are. LLMs are not tools. Control, sensory feedback, intention, intimacy, continuous direction, expertise etc are all missing from LLM use. LLMs are not wielded. LLMs are automation . automation - (of a device or process) working by itself with little or no direct human control. A drive-thru is not a tool for cooking, it is automation for avoiding cooking. LLMs are not tools with which you write code - they are automation with which you avoid writing code, to which you abdicate writing code. You don't direct the action of an LLM - you make requests and it acts on its own, without your energy or continuous direction. This request/automation cycle is not wielding, it's not control, it's not continuous, it's without feedback. What you are doing while using automation, instead of learning real-world truths, is attempting to divine the details du jour of some automaton. And striving to game them - e.g. ordering a custom burger (no onions) in order to get a freshly made one. Or filling voodoo.md with just the right

articles.title: Finding a $90,000 Remote Code Execution Vulnerability in Google
articles.content: How I found it I was mapping the OAuth flow that Google’s developer docs sites all share. You hit /oauth2authorize , it sets a Flask session cookie and redirects you to Google’s sign-in page. No account needed: curl -s -D headers.txt -o /dev/null \ 'https://developers.google.com/oauth2authorize?return_url=%2F' The cookie is what caught my eye. Flask’s usual three-part session=<payload>.<timestamp>.<signature> , but about 1,200 bytes, way more than you need for a CSRF token and a return URL. So I decoded it. Flask session cookies are signed, not encrypted, so the contents are right there for anyone holding one. The leading dot means the payload is zlib-compressed: import base64 import json import pickletools import zlib payload, timestamp, signature = cookie.rsplit( "." , 2 ) def b64decode (value): return base64.urlsafe_b64decode(value + "=" * ( - len (value) % 4 )) compressed = payload.startswith( "." ) raw = b64decode(payload[ 1 :] if compressed else payload) session = json.loads(zlib.decompress(raw) if compressed else raw) That gave me: { "_permanent" : true , "google_oauth2_csrf_token" : "..." , "google_oauth2_flow_<csrf>" : { " b" : "..." } } The " b" key is Flask tagging a bytes value. Base64-decoding it gave me a pickle, and pickletools.dis printed an oauth2client.client.OAuth2WebServerFlow object with its fields: client_id = "<redacted>.apps.googleusercontent.com" client_secret = b"<redacted>" The cookie contained a pickle-serialized payload, which was bad enough on its own. It also carried Google’s OAuth client_id and client_secret in plaintext. (The secret is redacted here; it was still live at the time of writing.) I tried the client secret as the Flask SECRET_KEY , and the signature on the issued cookie validated against it. The signing key was stored inside the object it signs. One secret, two jobs A client secret leaking in a cookie is a finding on its own. The part that mattered was that the same value verified the signature, so I nailed that down properly instead of trusting a lucky guess. Flask signs through itsdangerous with the cookie-session key derivation, so I recomputed the signature offline: import hmac derived_key = hmac.digest(client_secret, b "cookie-session" , "sha1" ) expected = hmac.digest( derived_key, f " { payload } . { timestamp } " .encode(), "sha1" , ) expected came out byte-for-byte identical to the signature on the cookie I’d been handed seconds earlier. To be sure it wasn’t a fluke I flipped one character of the signature (rejected) and re-signed the original payload with the recovered secret (accepted). Session integrity was gone. I could set every key and value in the session and still produce a signature the server would take. From forged cookie to code execution The callback reads the flow back out of the session and unpickles it: session cookie -> verify Flask signature -> read google_oauth2_flow_<csrf> -> base64-decode the bytes -> pickle.loads(...) That pickle.loads is only “safe” as long as nobody els

articles.title: I'm sorry, but you still have to think
articles.content: Written by Piotr Sarnacki on October 11, 2026 I'm sorry, but you still have to think DHH, the creator of the Ruby on Rails framework, decided to rewrite Campfire Once from Ruby on Rails to Rust. Or rather ask a clanker to do it for him, as he can't stand reading or writing the Rust code himself. After that he added rewrites in other languages , like Elixir and Go. This is very interesting to me, as it's a very good insight into the results of someone using AI agents without reading the code. In this case, that someone has also a lot of prior programming experience. And the results are... well, not very encouraging if you are hoping you can stop reading the code, or stop thinking altogether anytime soon. There are multiple problems with the rewrites, but let's start with non-functional differences cause they nicely show something that a lot of people seem to not realize: if your prompt is not specific enough, many decisions are a coin flip. This is because a whole lot of questions don't have a single correct answer. Do we want to keep backwards compatibility? Do we care more about latency or throughput? How much memory can the system use under load? Is loosing new content notifications after a crash acceptable? You may not care about them, or at least some of them, but they will be implicitly answered when an LLM implements what you think you want. If you look into the rewrites closer, you will quickly see that they treat backwards compatibility and other constraints differently. The Rust version doesn't maintain 100% backwards compatibility, for example it drops the CSRF token so that caching is easier. It also dropped Redis in favour of in-process queues, for example for notifications. Elixir rewrite is much closer to the Rails original. This already makes the comparison pretty much useless, as these differences are language independent. It's not like a clanker heard "rewrite in Elixir" and chose to keep 100% backwards compatibility because of the language that has been used. But it gets even better! If you looked at the code, and yeah, I know, we should not be reading code anymore, you would quickly notice a lot of the things are not great. For example, I've seen people complaining that Elixir's version got a single process sequentially processing all of the SQL queries, even if these were reads that could be running concurrently. That's a fair complaint, but DHH seems to think it's not the best look for Elixir that the clanker couldn't write performant code. Not sure if I agree when I look at the Rust version. Cause in the Rust version some of the database operations are not async, which in some cases may be worse. You see, in Rust, when using an async runtime, the scheduling is not preemptive, but rather cooperative. If a task doesn't yield, no other task can run on the same worker thread. articles.title: Type-safe HTML templating in Zig
articles.content: I’ve done a lot of web development over the years. I started around the year 2000, just after PHP 3.0 was released and started taking over the web world. I’ve used all kinds of approaches for generating HTML: raw PHP, string concatenation in Python, Smarty templates in PHP, Template Toolkit in Perl, and Jinja/Django templates in Python. Then, as the world moved on to SPAs and JavaScript frameworks, I stopped working on frontends. Two years ago, I picked up Zig, and I’d never have imagined I’d be considering web development in such a low-level language. But as I was building my own ecosystem with zio and Dusty , I realized it’s not that far-fetched. I built these libraries for API backends, where the output is JSON or MessagePack, but then I saw that with proper use of arena allocators, even web development is actually manageable, since you don’t need to remember to deallocate all the strings that are typically involved. And with Zig’s comptime, you can build very high-level interfaces without losing the performance benefits. And with the help of htmx or Datastar , you can even build SPAs without touching JavaScript/TypeScript, which I promised myself I’d never do. That said, one thing was still missing: templating. String concatenation was not an option, I didn’t want to go back to the pre-2000 CGI days. I had a few requirements for a templating library: It has to be type-safe, with all inputs typed and checked at compile time. I’ve dealt with dynamic languages enough in my life, and I don’t want to deal with runtime template errors anymore. It has to be fast. No allocations, no intermediate state, just write the output to std.Io.Writer directly. It needs to have safe defaults. I don’t want to deal with XSS anymore, so all inputs have to be escaped by default. It should still feel like writing HTML. I didn’t want a Zig-based DSL I’d have to fight constantly. I couldn’t find any solution that would satisfy all these requirements. Then I saw Ziex and I was amazed. It never occurred to me that the JSX approach could be done outside of JavaScript. The developer experience Nurul Huda managed to build in Zig was just unimaginable to me. It didn’t fit my needs directly, because I didn’t want a WASM framework, but the syntax and his approach to integrating Zig code into templates gave me some ideas. Then, after further research, I discovered Templ for Go, and it was pretty obvious to me what I wanted to build. So, let me present zt (I’m not good at naming, sorry) . It’s an adaptation of Templ to Zig. The templates are parsed and transpiled to Zig code during zig build . That means you can import them directly from your app code, but also, perhaps even more importantly, the templates can import your app code. As a result, all parameters can be fully typed. If something can’t be rendered, the Zig compiler will tell you so. The generated code is fairly simple, all it does is write to a std.Io.Writer . You can write directly to a socket or accumulate the out

articles.title: Elon Musk Bragged About His Grok Lego Star Wars Haul. Then X Users Punked Him
articles.content: There's been a disturbance in the force. Only it's more like a farce. It seems that Elon Musk, while crowing on X about how useful his Grok Bot AI agent was in ordering some Lego Star Wars kits on Sunday, managed to reveal via a screenshot to his more than 240 million followers not only the 10-digit Lego order number of his purchase, but also what he paid for the sets, the delivery and billing addresses, the last four digits of his credit card, and the email address his bot used to buy the bricks from Lego . Faster than the Millennium Falcon making the jump to light speed, the inevitable happened. An X account holder named Enderman posted screenshots of interactions with Lego's customer service chatbot on its website, where the user seemingly managed—using the email and order number Musk kindly, but recklessly, provided—to get the system to cancel Musk's order. It’s a Trap! Within a couple of hours—possibly to see whether Enderman's scheme was actually successful—Musk replied and said his order had not been canceled after all. But by this point, the folly of posting the purchase details on his account must have been evident. For example, another X user went back to Lego's AI assistant, called “Sophia,” and supposedly used the same details to reopen the delivery, this time increasing the order count to 400 and changing the delivery address, all while using Musk's original payment method. “Perfect! I'll get your Lego adventure back on track,” Sophia replied, according to screenshots posted on X. Upping the ante to 400 sets could be seen as conservative, as a glance at WIRED's Spend Elon Musk’s Money tracker reveals that if you wanted to blow $1 trillion of Musk's cash on plastic bricks, it might have been possible to buy one billion $1,000 Death Star sets, each with 9,023 pieces. Lego declined to comment when WIRED contacted the company to confirm if such activity took place on Musk's personal Star Wars order. However, internal safeguards for Lego's AI assistant could have flagged unusual activity on the purchase, and so hopefully fleshy humans were tasked with checking the changes. In this post , Musk suggested that all brave users needed to do to let Grok buy stuff for them was upload a picture of their credit card so the bot could search the web for deals and then complete the purchase. articles.title: How Apple Puts Indigenous Languages on the iPhone Keyboard
articles.content: To save endangered languages, tech companies like Apple are working with Indigenous communities to meet the next generation where they type.
articles.summary: 苹果与土著社区合作，将濒危土著语言加入iPhone键盘，以在下一代打字场景中保护这些语言。

articles.title: Feds Got Warrants to Use Fake Cell Towers to Hunt Down Don Lemon’s Producer
articles.content: Investigators also sought permission to use an invasive surveillance tool called a cell-site simulators against journalist Georgia Fort and a Minnesota state Senate candidate.
articles.summary: 联邦调查人员获搜查令，使用伪基站追踪Don Lemon制片人，并申请对记者Georgia Fort及明尼苏达州参议员候选人使用手机监控工具。

articles.title: AlterMe Review: Fitness Built Around My DNA
articles.content: Six months with AlterMe’s smart ring and a fitness app helped me build better habits, but the genetic insights were less revealing than I’d hoped.
articles.summary: Wired记者体验AlterMe智能戒指和健身应用六个月，习惯养成有改善，但基因洞察效果不及预期。

articles.title: A New Anti-Aging Drug Looks to Turn Back the Clock on Skin Age
articles.content: After four weeks of using the cream, participants lowered the biological age of their skin by about two years on average.
articles.summary: 一款新型抗衰老面霜经四周使用后，参与者皮肤生物学年龄平均降低约两岁。

articles.title: Spotify More Than Doubled Monthly Code Changes as AI Accelerated Development
articles.content: Spotify reports that AI-assisted development more than doubled monthly merged changes, prompting a review of quality and reliability controls across its engineering organization. The company describes changes to testing, observability, rollback capacity, workload prioritization, and automated maintenance as it adapts to higher software change volume. By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: Spotify表示AI辅助开发使每月合并代码变更量翻倍以上，公司因此重新审视测试、可观测性、回滚和自动化维护等质量控制。

articles.title: Article: When Should You Use Liquid Clustering? Benchmarking Lakehouse Layout Strategies
articles.content: Physical data layout is one of the most consequential decisions in lakehouse engineering. The author compares Liquid Clustering, ZOrdering, and partitioning across four workload types on Delta Lake, uncovering two undocumented failure modes that likely affect production systems today and offering a decision framework for choosing the right layout strategy. By Kushal Kumar Vishwakarma
articles.summary: InfoQ文章在Delta Lake上对比Liquid Clustering、ZOrdering和分区策略，发现两种未记录故障模式，可能影响现有生产系统。

articles.title: Podcast: What Does It Really Mean To Program With AI: A Conversation with Joy Ebertz
articles.content: In this podcast, Michael Stiefel spoke to Joy Ebertz about how the use of artificial intelligence is changing the way architects and developers do their jobs. Focusing on the long term success of the business is one of the most neglected tasks of an architect. This task becomes particularly important as the nature of artificial intelligence changes the landscape of software development. By Joy Ebertz
articles.summary: InfoQ播客中Joy Ebertz与主持人探讨AI如何改变架构师和开发者的工作方式，强调架构师需关注业务长期成功。

articles.title: Presentation: You Can't Trust Your AI Bill. And Neither Can I
articles.content: Erik Peterson discusses why AI spend is eclipsing cloud bills, triggering a major software engineering cost crisis. He explains tokenmaxxing, unit economics, forced developer promotions, and why fully autonomous AI will write, deploy, and govern code by 2028. By Erik Peterson
articles.summary: Erik Peterson在演讲中指出AI支出正超过云账单，引发软件工程成本危机，并预测到2028年全自主AI将编写、部署和治理代码。

articles.title: React 19.3: Adds a browser() API, Giving Client-Only Rendering a First-Class Name
articles.content: React 19.3 was released on September 9, introducing several features including the react-dom browser() API. This API allows components to opt out of server-side rendering, addressing issues with components that rely on client-specific data. It provides a cleaner solution for managing hydration mismatches and supports conditional data fetching, enhancing flexibility for developers. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: React 19.3发布，新增react-dom的browser() API，允许组件退出服务端渲染，为纯客户端渲染提供更清晰的解决方案。

articles.title: Java News Roundup: Grails 8, Open Liberty, GlassFish, Infinispan, LangChain4j, Spock
articles.content: This week's Java roundup for October 5th, 2026, features news highlighting: OpenJDK JEPs Proposed to Target for JDK 28; Lazy Constants elevated to Candidate status; the GA releases of Apache Grails 8.0 and Open Liberty 20.0.0.10; point releases of TornadoVM, Infinispan, LangChain4j and Spock; and a maintenance release of GlassFish. By Michael Redlich
articles.summary: 本周Java资讯：JDK 28相关JEP进入目标阶段，Lazy Constants升为候选，Grails 8.0和Open Liberty 20.0.0.10正式发布，多个项目发布点版本。

articles.title: GitLab 19.4 Adds Goal-Driven Agents and Tighter Cost Controls
articles.content: GitLab has released version 19.4 of its DevSecOps platform, adding a goal-driven mode to GitLab Duo CLI, three hosted open-weight models, a larger set of Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, and more detailed controls for AI spending. By Matt Saunders
articles.summary: GitLab 发布 DevSecOps 平台 19.4 版，为 Duo CLI 加入目标驱动模式、三款开源权重模型和更多 MCP 工具，并强化 AI 成本管控。

articles.title: Xcode 27.2 Introduces an Agent- and Merge-Friendly JSON Format for Project Configuration
articles.content: Apple is introducing a new JSON-based format for Xcode project configuration files, replacing the traditional property-list-based format. Available in Xcode 27.2, the new format aims to improve readability, simplify maintenance, and make project configuration easier for AI coding agents to understand and modify. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: 苹果在 Xcode 27.2 中引入基于 JSON 的项目配置格式，取代传统 plist，提升可读性并便于 AI 编码代理理解项目结构。

articles.title: Context Language Models: Self-Managing Context to Improve Performance and Reduce Compute Costs
articles.content: Researchers from Meta, MIT, and the University of Washington introduce Context Language Models (CLMs), a new approach that enables language models to manage and edit their own context rather than relying on predefined mechanisms for summarization, compression, and information retrieval, reporting substantial gains in both performance and computational efficiency. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: Meta、MIT 与华盛顿大学提出上下文语言模型（CLM），让模型自行管理编辑上下文，无需预设摘要压缩机制，可提升性能并降低算力成本。

articles.title: Foresight AI Brings Gremlin Agents to Reliability Engineering
articles.content: Reliability management company Gremlin has announced the general availability of Foresight AI, an agentic product that analyses services for potential failures, recommends changes and reruns tests to check that a fix works. By Matt Saunders
articles.summary: 可靠性管理公司 Gremlin 正式发布 Foresight AI，可分析服务潜在故障、推荐修复方案并重跑测试验证修复效果。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第536期：顶尖 AI 模型未能通过自主开展 AI 研究的测试，同时探讨 AI 治理、军事规划与个人电脑落地等议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第535期：因成本过高，企业开始转向更便宜的模型，同时大规模部署进入日常使用，AI 受限或被移除的场景也在增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第534期：高校 IT 负责人首次将 AI 列为首要任务，剑桥拒绝 Turnitin 新条款，学生使用 AI 已成现实而非未来议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #533: Meta tested human callers behind its AI phone agent
articles.content: The AI story of September 22–28 was not simply that agents became more capable. It was that their hidden handoffs became visible: a supposedly automated call could reach a contractor, a supposedly private prompt or image could reach a reviewer, a monitor could detect an agent long before a person stopped it, and a local app flaw could inherit every permission a user had granted. The new AI Weekly Who’s Who census points to one practical question: when an agent crosses a boundary, who knows—and who can still intervene?
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第533期：Meta 被曝其 AI 电话代理背后有人工接线员，揭示所谓自动化代理存在隐藏的人工转接环节。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #531: AI labs shipped agents before agreeing how to report failures
articles.content: The AI story of September 14–20 was not one spectacular model launch. It was the machinery around agents becoming visible: people reading private chats, models writing instructions into their own memory, plugins updating beneath users, and regulators asking how to stop a system after release. The latest AI Weekly Who’s Who census surfaced 535 expert-shared links. We ranked them by consequence and reader relevance, not by raw share count. Here is what mattered last week—and, more importantly, what could move the story from September 22–28.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第531期：AI 实验室在未就故障上报方式达成一致前便已发布代理产品，隐私读取、记忆写入与监管问题随之浮现。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #530: Applied AI This Week
articles.content: Companies are giving AI specific jobs: checking security cameras, helping farmers understand their records, searching satellite images, and preparing sales quotes. This edition explains how those tools work, who can use them, and what companies have reported so far.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第530期：企业为 AI 分配具体任务，如监控摄像头、辅助农户理解记录、搜索卫星图像和准备销售报价。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #529: OpenAI faces 50-plus lawsuits over alleged ChatGPT harm
articles.content: Thirty new complaints come from survivors of a Canadian school shooting. They accuse OpenAI of failing to warn police; the company disputes key claims.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第529期：OpenAI 因 ChatGPT 涉嫌造成伤害面临 50 多起诉讼，其中 30 起来自加拿大校园枪击案幸存者，指控其未警告警方。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #528: What are companies building with AI? An Applied AI Deep Dive
articles.content: We went looking for what companies are actually building with AI. The answer was not more chatbots. It was drones carrying diagnostic samples, driverless Frito-Lay trucks, AI-guided flight paths, repair copilots, and rugged GPU laptops in Ukraine. We reviewed 136 use cases from the last 20 days. The biggest surprise: only 38 included a reported outcome.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第528期：企业实际用 AI 构建的并非聊天机器人，而是诊断样本无人机、无人驾驶卡车、维修副驾等，共梳理 136 个用例。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #527: Schools are choosing opposite futures for AI
articles.content: One University of Chicago curriculum is removing AI-assisted writing from the classroom. Alpha School is expanding a model that puts adaptive software at the center of the academic day. The strongest signal in the latest Who’s Who Global Edition is that education is moving past general principles and into incompatible operating designs.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 第527期：学校对 AI 选择截然相反的道路，芝加哥大学课程移除 AI 辅助写作，Alpha School 则以自适应软件为核心。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #525: Nvidia may buy into Perplexity above $30B before Wednesday's earnings
articles.content: The Information reports that Nvidia is discussing an equity investment in Perplexity at a valuation above $30 billion. Perplexity's annualized revenue has reportedly passed $750 million, up from less than $250 million at the start of 2026. Separately, Bloomberg says SoftBank plans a record ¥1 trillion, or $6.3 billion, retail bond to help repay the bridge loan behind its OpenAI stake and fund more AI deals. Put together, the signals expose next week's capital split: the chip supplier is moving toward the product layer, while the frontier investor is asking Japanese savers to finance its bets. Nvidia reports Wednesday at 5 p.m. ET. Listen for whether management now talks like a supplier, an investor, or both.
articles.summary: 据报英伟达正洽谈以超 300 亿美元估值入股 Perplexity，后者年化收入已超 7.5 亿美元；软银另计划创纪录的万亿日元投资。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: NanoClaw 作者 Gavriel Cohen 讲述一个 40 小时周末项目如何成为爆红开源项目，并发展为容器隔离的企业级 AI 公司。

articles.title: Changelog IRL @ PlanetScale (Sept 17, 2026)
articles.content: Changelog is taking over PlanetScale's HQ We’re getting together IRL!! On Thursday, September 17th, Changelog is taking over PlanetScale’s HQ in San Francisco for an evening of short talks and conversations about AI, developer tools and what people are building. PlanetScale HQ, 108 Natoma St, San Francisco.
articles.summary: Changelog 将于 9 月 17 日在 PlanetScale 旧金山总部举办线下活动，围绕 AI、开发工具与开发者实践展开短演讲与交流。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com 联合创始人 Peer Richelsen 做客播客，讨论开源仓库可能已被暗中破坏的猜想，以及 AI 如何改变知识获取门槛。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: PlanetScale 推出 5 美元 Postgres 服务，重构 Vitess，支持代理提交 schema 变更并秒级回滚 500TB 表，引发是否开源的讨论。

articles.title: Canary tokens and digital tripwires
articles.content: Haroon Meer is back! Haroon is the Founder of Thinkst, the ~50-person bootstrapped company behind Canary and Canarytokens — honeypots and tripwires you sprinkle inside your network and forget about until an attacker touches one. We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.
articles.summary: Thinkst 创始人介绍 Canary 和 Canarytokens 蜜罐工具，用于在内部网络布置数字绊线，检测攻击者触碰行为。

articles.title: From open source hits to OpenAI
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Max Stoiber, currently working on ChatGPT's plugin directory and app platform at OpenAI. We discuss the hundreds of open source projects nobody remembers alongside the big ones like react-boilerplate and styled-components, how Spectrum became part of GitHub and eventually helped shape GitHub Discussions, the founder growth that came from building Stellate, the GraphQL cache that turned into a dual acquisition by Shopify and The Guild, and why ChatGPT apps feel like a new surface for software.
articles.summary: Max Stoiber 分享从开源项目 react-boilerplate、styled-components 到加入 OpenAI 负责 ChatGPT 插件目录的经历。

articles.title: MCP on Code Mode
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Matt Carey about Code Mode and how most of us have been thinking about MCP all wrong. Matt works on the Agents SDK and MCP at Cloudflare — we discuss how server-side Code Mode lets one MCP server expose all ~2,500 Cloudflare API endpoints in about 1,000 tokens of context, the dynamic Worker loader that runs model-written code safely in a V8 isolate, Matt's own workflow with Claude, where memory fits into the future of agents, and his Zaggy git wrapper that keeps agents from force-pushing his repos.
articles.summary: Cloudflare 的 Matt Carey 介绍 Code Mode 如何让单个 MCP 服务器以约 1000 token 暴露 2500 个 API 端点。

articles.title: Automation at the speed of Swamp
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Adam Jacob, founder of System Initiative and creator of Swamp, about what happens when AI agents change the entire shape of software development. We discuss how he went from an 18-person team down to five and shipped Swamp 900 times in four weeks, why he brought User Acceptance Testing (UAT) testing back from the 90s, why software architecture (and domain-driven design) suddenly matters more than knowing how to write code, the live demo where I pointed Swamp at my Proxmox box and watched it write its own automation (blew my mind!!), and why he'll never accept a pull request to Swamp, ever.
articles.summary: System Initiative 创始人 Adam Jacob 讲述 AI 代理改变软件开发形态，团队从 18 人缩减至 5 人，四周内发布 Swamp 900 次。

articles.title: Bitwarden CLI compromised
articles.content: Bitwarden's CLI got hit by the Checkmarx supply-chain campaign, TypeScript 7.0 beta lands with the Go-rewritten compiler running ~10x faster than 6.0, and pgBackRest lost its maintainer of thirteen years leaving anyone running production Postgres with a real dependency-trust task this week. We've also got Ubuntu 26.04 LTS shipping with TPM-backed full-disk encryption, and Matz dropping Spinel as an AOT path that takes Ruby to native binaries. This week was a good reminder that the tools we depend on are all moving at once. Security, performance, and maintenance aren't isolated threads.
articles.summary: Bitwarden CLI 遭 Checkmarx 供应链攻击，TypeScript 7.0 beta 编译器提速约 10 倍，pgBackRest 维护者离职引发依赖信任问题。

articles.title: Exploring with agents
articles.content: Today on the show I’m talking with Amelia Wattenberger — designer, data-viz veteran, ex-GitHub Next, and now designing Intent at Augment Code. What if the last 30% of any software project is about to become the hardest part you’ve ever done? That’s the argument Amelia is making today. We discuss the identity crisis developers are having as agents take over the keyboard, the epic redesign of developer tooling in this agent-first world, the arc from autocomplete to chat to CLI back to UI, why Intent treats a workspace as their core primitive not a chat thread, the tradeoffs between one-worktree-per-agent vs. one-worktree-per-task, and why she thinks prototyping just got easier but finishing got harder.
articles.summary: 设计师 Amelia Wattenberger 探讨 AI 代理时代软件开发最后 30% 的工作为何可能成为最难的部分。

articles.title: Firefox 158 Now Available With JPEG-XL Support By Default
articles.content: Firefox 158 is now available with JPEG XL image support enabled by default, making .jxl images a standard part of the browser rather than an experimental feature. The release also adds JPEG XL to Firefox's default image Accept header, improves Smart Window form filling, and brings new CSS typed-arithmetic support for developers. Phoronix reports: At long last, Firefox 158 is ready to go with JPEG-XL image support as an alternative to the likes of WebP, JPEG, PNG, and GIF. The default HTTP Accept header for image requests also now supports "image/jxl" for the JPEG-XL image format. Prior releases of Firefox had JPEG-XL gated by an experimental option. Firefox 158 also now supports filling forms faster in Smart Window when clicking into a form field or selecting Fill from sources. On the developer side, CSS typed arithmetic are now supported to use functions like calc() to divide two values of the same data type even if of different units. Developer changes and release binaries can be found at their respective links. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: Firefox 158 发布，默认启用 JPEG XL 图像支持，并改进智能窗口表单填充和 CSS 类型化算术。

articles.title: Epic Games Delays Disney Project, Asks Developers To Use More AI
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Bloomberg: Epic Games delayed the release of an upcoming video-game collaboration with Walt Disney and told its developers to use more artificial intelligence tools to finish the game, according to people familiar with the project. The title had been slated for release in March, but is now delayed with no new date communicated, said the people familiar, who asked to not be identified because they weren't authorized to speak publicly. Developers on the game, a shooter featuring characters from the Marvel and Star Wars franchises, were instructed to implement an "AI first" production model using tools such as Anthropic's Claude. Humans will then manage and guide that work. "No more hand-written code," one of the game's directors told staff in an internal message reviewed by Bloomberg. The director added that all art for the game would be "generated with full AI workflows." Even before this announcement, the maker of the popular Fortnite game had been pushing hard for the use of AI across all of its divisions. But this is the first time a major video-game company has attempted to build a title primarily with AI. "We're embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do," said Jake Jones, communications director at Epic Games, in a statement to Bloomberg News. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: Epic Games 推迟与迪士尼合作游戏，并要求开发者更多使用 AI 工具完成开发。

articles.title: Mark Zuckerberg Says Meta Has Reached AI 'Frontier', Rejects Calls For Slowdown
articles.content: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg says the company has reached the AI "frontier" with its new Muse Wonder model and will be offered as a closed, paid product for businesses. Zuckerberg also rejected calls for an industry-wide slowdown, arguing that AI can be managed with conventional guardrails as Meta continues spending heavily on models, infrastructure, and talent. The Financial Times reports: Speaking with the FT as Meta releases its Muse Wonder AI model on Monday, the billionaire chief executive claimed the new system was "going to allow much more sophisticated behaviours that are at the frontier of what is being done in the AI field." [...] "Getting to this point both required a large amount of compute and investment, and a lot of very rigorous scientific work by the group working on it over an extended period of time," said Zuckerberg. [...] Meta said Muse Wonder outperforms Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on some technical benchmarks. It said the new model can be used to carry out complex tasks from "understanding a lease to making sense of financial or health information." However, Muse Wonder will also be "closed," with its best versions sold directly to businesses. That pits it against Anthropic and OpenAI for corporate AI contracts in a serious test of its ambitions. Zuckerberg signaled further spending as Meta was "already working on the next step up," adding that its model development would "probably feel like it'll go quite a bit faster from here." However, he also shrugged off mounting fears that the technology was advancing at a rate that will soon surpass human control. [...] The Meta chief declined to be drawn on his figure for "P(doom)" -- a much-discussed Silicon Valley term to describe the probability that AI will lead to mass destruction. Instead, he argued that responsibility should fall on the individual lab to ensure model safety. "I'm much closer to the belief that AI is a technology that can be engineered with nor
articles.summary: 扎克伯格称 Meta 凭借 Muse Wonder 模型已达 AI 前沿，将作为闭源付费产品提供给企业，并拒绝行业放缓呼吁。

articles.title: Google's Fitbit Edge Debuts a Replaceable Battery, Brings Back the Screen
articles.content: Google has introduced the $179 Fitbit Edge, a new fitness tracker with a 1.34-inch OLED display, built-in GPS, ECG support, week-long battery life, and Fitbit's first user-replaceable battery. "And unlike the Pixel Watch, it's compatible with Android and iPhones via the Google Health app," reports Wired. From the report: The Edge has a user-replaceable battery, a Fitbit first, aligning with Google's efforts to make its Pixel Watch more repairable. (Likely also due to new battery regulations set to take effect next year in the European Union.) Repair options will vary by region and availability. If you find the Pixel Watch's round face too bulky, the Edge's capsule-shaped alternative might suit smaller wrists better. If the Charge 6's 1.04-inch display was too small, the Edge upgrades it to a larger 1.34-inch screen. articles.title: Hackers Heat French Supermarket Fridges, Sparking Fires and Spoiling Food
articles.content: Hackers remotely manipulated connected refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets, reportedly pushing some fridges and freezers to 50C (122F), spoiling food and even sparking fires. According to Reuters, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu ordered a cybersecurity investigation into the hacks, with similar incidents reported in Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany, and Belgium. In France, Carrefour reported 80 affected stores, Monoprix said 5% of its locations were hit, and Les Mousquetaires said refrigerators at roughly 150 Intermarche stores were heated to 50C for six hours. From the report: Supermarket cold aisles are typically run by control panels that manage an entire store's fridges and freezers and can be accessed over the internet, which lets maintenance companies adjust them from anywhere. The source close to Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss. Danfoss said it was "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems." The affected units "were running outdated firmware," Danfoss said, adding that it had "long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions." On August 9, cybersecurity firm Claroty's Team82 published research detailing vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A controller. According to the report, software updates issued by Danfoss addressed issues that could have allowed attackers to bypass authentication controls and execute code on compromised devices. articles.content: A study of more than 700 software firms found that AI coding agents significantly increase the amount of code developers produce, but not the amount of software companies actually ship. Ars Technica reports: A recent study (PDF) of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant "bottleneck" for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in "little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment" by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is "absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process"; as "the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments." The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. articles.title: Amazon In Talks To Buy AI Startup Decart For Around $7 Billion
articles.content: Amazon is reportedly in talks to acquire AI startup Decart in a deal that could value the company at up to $7 billion. Decart's DOS software helps developers optimize AI models for different processors in weeks rather than months, a capability that could be particularly useful to AWS as it pushes its own Trainium chips. SiliconANGLE reports: The company has developed software called DOS, which can help developers to speed up AI training and inference workloads by optimizing their neural networks to run on a specific processor. In most AI workloads, developers must optimize a neural network for the chip they plan to run it on. This process used to take months, but with DOS, the workflow necessary to do this can be compressed into just a couple of weeks. As a result, companies can use Decart's software to shift AI workloads to different processors if their requirements change, or if chip availability becomes an issue. In addition to DOS, Decart is also a model developer, responsible for creating the Lucy and Oasis world models, which are designed to generate and simulate realistic three-dimensional environments for video games, robotic training and other use cases. It's still possible another suitor could emerge and outbid Amazon. Last month, Anthropic PBC was reportedly engaged in talks to buy Decart, according to a report by Bloomberg. articles.title: Q3 2026 Was Historically Bad For PC Shipments
articles.content: PC shipments fell 20.1% year over year to 62.7 million units in the third quarter of 2026, the worst Q3 decline IDC has recorded. "The top three PC makers -- Lenovo, Dell, and HP -- also saw their shipments fall by over 20% year over year," reports PCMag. From the report: "If looking at all quarters, then we have seen other quarters in recent years with larger declines, such as 2022Q4, which was -28.2%, and 2023Q1, which was -28.7%. Both were coming off pandemic highs," IDC Director Jitesh Ubrani told PCMag in an email. The numbers aren't a great sign, since third-quarter PC shipments usually outpace those in the second quarter as vendors introduce new products ahead of the holiday shopping season. Instead, PC shipments were at 62.7 million units, down 9.1% from the previous quarter. [...] Of course, the downturn isn't a surprise. IDC and other research firms have warned that the ongoing AI-driven memory shortage threatens to sap demand for PCs and phones due to soaring memory and storage costs. "What we're seeing is the result of the strong first half pull-in. Vendors and channels loaded up on inventory early in the year to get ahead of [memory-related] price hikes, and that has thrown off the usual seasonality, where Q3 is typically larger than Q2," Ubrani said in a report covering IDC's preliminary estimates for the quarter. In one bright spot, Ubrani said vendors and retailers might cut prices to generate interest and clear out products they have in stock. "Channels are now worried about carrying too much inventory into a market where high prices are suppressing demand. That could translate into promotions and some short-term relief for consumers, but we don't expect pricing anywhere near what it was a year ago. Prices will remain elevated," he added. In the benchmark , it was about 3.6x faster than Immer with the same settings and 6.6x faster with each library's defaults across 97 workloads. How does Mutative compare with the spread operation (hand-written reducers)? Mutative copies each object at most once per update, however many changes a recipe makes. articles.title: Type-safe OpenAPI requests that follow your document exactly
articles.content: openapi-chain compiles the serialization rules an OpenAPI document declares (parameter style , explode , allowReserved and content , request media types, and form and multipart Encoding Objects) and applies them to every request. A build-time CLI generates types and metadata scoped to the paths you call, so large documents stay affordable to type-check and to ship. Calls use a fluent path API with no generated endpoint code and no runtime dependencies. The pnpm monorepo contains three publishable packages: openapi-chain , @openapi-chain/cli , and @openapi-chain/query . The runtime keeps its existing package name and entry points. See the package migration guide for CLI and query import changes and release availability. The first request below uses the Items schema . Your chain follows your own schema: static path segments become properties, {parameters} become function calls, and HTTP methods become request functions. Exact wire serialization: the strict client sends what the document specifies and rejects representations it cannot encode instead of guessing. The wire comparison executes 20 declarations through both clients: openapi-fetch 0.17.0 sends a request with different values, media type or missing parameters in 16 of them, and differs only in percent-encoding or list spacing in 3 more. Scoped generation for large documents: one CLI config produces full declarations, a path scope and matching runtime metadata. On the pinned GitHub REST document, scoping a 40-operation consumer reduced openapi-chain's TypeScript 7 check time from 0.49 s to 0.045 s ( real-schema measurements ). Typed requests and responses: infer parameters, request media types and status-correlated results from the selected operation. Keep openapi-fetch if you already use it: openapi-chain/openapi-fetch applies the same serialization to an existing openapi-fetch client ( adapter guide ). Small schema-free core: the default client has a 3.5 KiB gzip budget , enforced by a reproducible size check ; its bundle size and per-request overhead are in the same range as openapi-fetch ( client comparison ). Customizable requests: operation-typed extensions and Fetch-compatible transports support application-specific serialization, authentication and parsing. When to choose openapi-chain Choose the strict client when your document declares non-default parameter styles, parameter content , cookie parameters, non-JSON media types or form and multipart encoding, and the server depends on them. Choose the CLI's scoped generation when a large document makes type-checking or metadata delivery expensive. If your API only uses JSON bodies and default parameter styles, openapi-fetch and openapi-chain's core are comparable in size and speed; pick the call style you prefer. Without scoping, openapi-chain's fluent types cost more to check than openapi-fetch's on the measured GitHub and Stripe documents. For a published release with this API: pnpm add openapi-chain pnpm add -D @openapi-chain/cli S

First when you pick the tool stack (or get onboarded to it), then every time things drift apart: the linter disagrees with the formatter, CI runs different commands than you do locally, one repo is two majors behind another, and the person who originally set it up is on vacation. Teams with more than a handful of repositories usually end up building internal scripts to paper over this, which then need their own maintainers. articles.title: Node.JS Built-Ins That Replaced NPM Packages
articles.content: Home / Node.js Node.js built-ins that replaced npm packages By Flavio Copes Sep 20, 2026 Twelve Node.js built-ins that replace axios, nodemon, dotenv, jest, chalk, glob and more, with their stability in Node 24 and one gotcha each. ~~~ Open a package.json from a few years ago and you’ll find the same names in almost every one. axios , nodemon , dotenv , jest , chalk , uuid , rimraf . Node.js now ships a built-in for each of them. Here are twelve of those built-ins, with the package each one replaces, the shortest example that runs, how stable it is in the current LTS line, and the one thing the old package still does that the built-in doesn’t. Several of these changed status in the last year, so I checked every claim against the Node 24 API docs (24.21.0, the Active LTS line as of September 2026) and ran every example on Node 26.0.0, which is what node --version prints on my Mac. Node 22 is in maintenance until April 2027, Node 20 reached end of life on April 30, 2026, and Node 26 becomes the next LTS on October 28, 2026. Where Node 22 and 24 differ, I say so. A quick reminder on how Node labels its APIs. Stability 2 is stable. Stability 1 is experimental, with sub-levels: 1.0 is early development, 1.1 is active development, 1.2 is a release candidate. Anything experimental can change or disappear in a minor release, so the number matters if you’re putting it in production. 1. node:sqlite replaces better-sqlite3 For years the way to use SQLite from Node was better-sqlite3 , a native addon you had to compile (or download a prebuilt binary for) on every install. Node 22.5 added a SQLite driver to core. Like better-sqlite3 , it’s synchronous, so the code reads top to bottom with no await . import { DatabaseSync } from 'node:sqlite' const db = new DatabaseSync ( '/Users/flavio/notes.db' ) db. exec ( 'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, body TEXT)' ) const insert = db. prepare ( 'INSERT INTO notes (body) VALUES (?)' ) insert. run ( 'Buy espresso beans' ) console. log (db. prepare ( 'SELECT * FROM notes' ). all ()) The module only exists under the node: prefix, a plain import 'sqlite' fails. Status in Node 24: 1.2, release candidate , since 24.15.0. It prints no warning. In Node 22 it’s still 1.1, active development (the --experimental-sqlite flag went away in 22.13, the label didn’t), so a server on Node 22 is running an API the docs describe as “nearing minimum viability”. Where it does less: better-sqlite3 has db.transaction(fn) , which wraps a function in BEGIN , COMMIT and ROLLBACK for you, and node:sqlite has nothing like it. You write those three statements yourself in a try / catch . I show the pattern in node:sqlite: SQLite built into Node.js , and the free SQLite course covers transactions and indexes in more depth. 2. node:test and node:assert replace Jest and Mocha Jest was the default test runner for a long time, and I have a whole post on it from 2018. Mocha plus Chai was the other common pair. Both are still fine. B

articles.title: Tibetan-Singing-Bowls: Strike or rub a set of virtual Tibetan singing bowls - synthesized in the browser with Web Audio, with the beating overtones of the real thing
articles.content: Play a set of virtual Tibetan singing bowls right in your browser. Strike a bowl, or hold it down to draw the tone out the way a mallet circles the rim. The sound is synthesized live, so there are no audio files to load, and it works offline. Use headphones or good speakers. Seven bowls are tuned to a scale, each with its own color. Tap or click a bowl to strike it. Switch to Sing and hold a bowl down to make it swell and sustain, then let go to let it fade. The number keys 1 to 7 play the bowls from the keyboard, and you can play several at once. Tuning : a seven-note chakra scale (C to B, one bowl per chakra) or a pentatonic scale, in the low, middle or high octave, with A at 440 Hz or 432 Hz. Sound : volume and room reverb. Spectrum : a live view of the sound, so you can watch the overtones rise and fade. Sound bath : press start and pick 5, 10, 20 or 30 minutes, and the bowls play by themselves, one strike at a time, with silence in between. A struck bowl rings at its fundamental plus overtones at about 2.7, 5.2 and 8.3 times that pitch. Those overtones are not whole-number multiples, which is why a bowl sounds like a bell and not like a string. Each partial is made of two sine oscillators a fraction of a hertz apart, so it swells and fades a few times a second: that beating is the "wah-wah" of a real bowl. Higher partials die away faster. The result goes through a synthesized room reverb and a compressor. This is a model of the sound and not a recording. The bowls are not meant as a medical treatment, and the chakra colors are a common convention, not a measurement. The pages are plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with the Web Audio API, with no dependencies and no build step. Just open index.html . It is also a small installable web app: add it to your home screen or desktop and it works offline. The bowls are drawn as SVG. The app logic is in js/bowls.js . Three color themes (dark, light and blue) are shared with my other projects. Your tuning, volume and other settings are kept in the browser's local storage. articles.content: Draw a mandala right in your browser. Whatever you draw is repeated around the center and mirrored, so a few loose strokes become a symmetric design. Save it as a PNG or as an SVG. No sign-up and no libraries. Press and drag on the drawing area with a mouse, a finger or a pen. Each stroke is repeated in every fold, and, if Mirror each fold is on, flipped inside each fold too, which is what gives a mandala its petal look. Folds : from 2 to 24 repeats around the center (12 by default).
